newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Opposition-led strike paralyses Pakistani province.
newsitem.headline: Opposition-led strike paralyses Pakistani province.

text.p: An opposition-led strike to mourn the killing of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's estranged brother Murtaza Bhutto paralysed Pakistan's southern province of Sindh on Thursday, including its capital and port city Karachi.
But police said there was no violence, which has marked many previous protest strikes in Karachi, Pakistan's commercial hub.
The strike was widespread in the interior of Sindh, paralysing life in Hyderabad and several other towns, witnesses there said.
Government departments, airline offices at the Karachi airport, the port and railways were open, but attendance was thin due to the absence of transport.
The strike had slowed the movement of petroleum products, edible oils, and other commodities to the countryside because of fear of arson, one transport operator said.
"Port operation, including import and export of cargo, was badly hit by thin attendance due to the strike," a port official said.
Witnesses said most cars and trucks stayed off the roads in the morning but traffic picked up in the afternoon.
The Karachi Stock Exchange opened but trading was dull as volume fell provisionally to 0.7 million, from Wednesday's 26 million and 100-share index fell 1.94 points, or 0.14 percent.
The Karachi Cotton Association did not issue its rates owing to a lack of quorum.
"Today's is one of the most effective strikes ever held in Karachi," a spokesman for Murtaza's breakaway Shaheed Bhutto group of the ruling Pakistan People's Party (PPP) told Reuters.
The strike was the 11th in the city this year, compared with more than 32 in 1995. Economists say the strikes have caused huge losses to the country's economy.

The strike call, first given by the Shaheed Bhutto group, was backed by the militant Mohajir National Movement (MQM) and eight other groups to protest against the killing of Murtaza and seven colleagues in a police shootout in Karachi on Friday.

The call was issued against what Murtaza's group called excessive force by security agencies. Police denied the charge. They blame Murtaza's group for Friday's shooting, saying they fired in self-defence.
Shaheed Bhutto says police fired without provocation, and Prime Minister Bhutto has said her younger brother was killed in a conspiracy against her family.
Armoured personnel carriers and paramilitary rangers patrolled violence-prone areas in the sprawling city of more than 12 million people, the witnesses said.
In Karachi, more than 300 people have been killed in ethnic, sectarian and political violence so far this year, far fewer than the 2,000 deaths recorded last year.
